subject: phy
title: Forces and Equilibrium
subtitle: Moments, couples, equilibrium and centre of gravity.
concept: A body is in equilibrium when the resultant force and resultant torque (moment) are both zero.
The moment of a force about a point equals force × perpendicular distance; a couple is a pair of equal, opposite, parallel forces.
The centre of gravity is the single point at which the entire weight of a body appears to act.

notes.heading: Moments and the Principle of Moments
items: The moment of a force about a pivot = force × perpendicular distance from the pivot to the line of action of the force (N m). Moments that rotate clockwise are positive by convention; anticlockwise are negative.
Principle of moments: for a body in rotational equilibrium, the sum of clockwise moments about any point equals the sum of anticlockwise moments about the same point.

A couple is a pair of equal, opposite, parallel forces — it produces pure rotation with no net translational force. The torque of a couple = F × d, where d is the perpendicular distance between the lines of action. This is independent of the choice of pivot.

notes.heading: Conditions for Equilibrium
items: A body is in equilibrium when: (1) the vector sum of all forces is zero (ΣF = 0 in all directions — translational equilibrium) and (2) the sum of moments about any point is zero (Στ = 0 — rotational equilibrium).
Tip: when solving for unknown forces, choose a pivot at the point where one unknown acts — it eliminates that unknown from the moments equation.

notes.heading: Centre of Gravity
items: The centre of gravity (CoG) is the single point at which the entire weight of an object appears to act. For uniform objects it coincides with the geometric centre.
To find the CoG experimentally: suspend the object from two different points and draw a plumb line from each. The CoG lies at the intersection.
Stability: an object topples if its CoG moves outside its base of support. A lower CoG and wider base both increase stability — this is why racing cars are built wide and low.

definitions.body: The product of a force and the perpendicular distance from the line of action of the force to the pivot: M = F × d⊥.
A pair of equal, opposite, parallel forces that produce rotation without translation; torque = F × d.
The point at which the entire weight of a body can be considered to act.
For a body in rotational equilibrium, the sum of clockwise moments equals the sum of anticlockwise moments about any point.

workedExamples.q: A uniform 4.0 m beam of weight 200 N is supported at each end. A 300 N load sits 1.0 m from the left end. Find the reactions at each support.

mistakes: Using the distance along the beam rather than the perpendicular distance from the pivot to the line of action of the force.
Forgetting to include the weight of the beam itself (acting at its centre) in moment calculations.
Confusing a couple (two forces, no net force) with a single force.
tips: To find an unknown support force: take moments about the other support — the unknown at your chosen pivot has zero moment.
A beam problem always needs: (1) ΣF = 0 vertically AND (2) Στ = 0 about one point.
Torque of a couple = F × d (not F × d from any pivot, but that is one way to calculate it — the result is the same from any point).

flashcards.q: State the two conditions for equilibrium.
flashcards.a: (1) ΣF = 0 in all directions. (2) Στ = 0 about any point.

flashcards.q: What is the torque of a couple?
flashcards.a: Torque = F × d, where F is one of the equal forces and d is the perpendicular distance between them.

flashcards.q: What is the principle of moments?
flashcards.a: For rotational equilibrium: sum of clockwise moments = sum of anticlockwise moments about any point.

flashcards.q: How do you locate the centre of gravity of an irregular shape experimentally?
flashcards.a: Suspend from two different points; draw plumb lines from each suspension point; the CoG is at the intersection.

flashcards.q: A force of 20 N acts at 30° to horizontal. What are its components?
flashcards.a: Horizontal: 20 cos30° = 17.3 N; Vertical: 20 sin30° = 10.0 N.
Two equal, opposite, parallel forces acting on a body; they produce pure rotation (no net translational force).

questions.q: A 10 N force acts at a perpendicular distance of 0.5 m from a pivot. What is the moment?
For a body in equilibrium, which conditions must BOTH be satisfied?
questions.exp: Both conditions are required: no resultant force (translational) AND no resultant torque (rotational).

questions.q: A 6 N and a 6 N equal, opposite, parallel force act 0.4 m apart. What is the couple's torque?
questions.exp: Torque of couple = F × d = 6 × 0.4 = 2.4 N m.

questions.q: Which change would make a standing object MORE stable?
questions.exp: Lowering the CoG and widening the base both increase stability; it is harder to topple an object with a low CoG.

questions.q: A uniform beam of weight 100 N is 2 m long, supported at both ends. Where does each support reaction act?
questions.exp: For a uniform beam with no additional load, symmetry means each support provides 50 N (half the weight).
